questions.title: Product Revenue
questions.description: Calculate the total revenue generated by each product across all orders, where revenue is defined as `unit_price * quantity * (1 - discount)`, summed at the product level.
questions.business_problem: The sales analytics team wants a breakdown of revenue contributed by every product in the catalog, after accounting for any discounts applied at the line-item level. This report feeds into product performance reviews and discontinuation decisions.
requirements: Calculate the total revenue generated by each product across all orders, where revenue is defined as `unit_price * quantity * (1 - discount)`, summed at the product level.
questions.reference_query:
SELECT
    p.product_id,
    p.product_name,
    ROUND(SUM(od.unit_price * od.quantity * (1 - od.discount))::numeric, 2) AS total_revenue
FROM products p
JOIN order_details od ON od.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;

questions.title: Category Revenue
questions.description: Calculate total discounted revenue generated by each product category by rolling up product-level sales through the category hierarchy.
questions.business_problem: Category managers need a consolidated view of how much revenue each product category generates after discounts, to compare category performance and guide merchandising strategy.
requirements: Calculate total discounted revenue generated by each product category by rolling up product-level sales through the category hierarchy.
questions.reference_query:
SELECT
    c.category_id,
    c.category_name,
    ROUND(SUM(od.unit_price * od.quantity * (1 - od.discount))::numeric, 2) AS total_revenue
FROM categories c
JOIN products p ON p.category_id = c.category_id
JOIN order_details od ON od.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY c.category_id, c.category_name
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;

questions.title: Top 10 Customers by Revenue
questions.description: Identify the 10 customers who have generated the highest total discounted revenue across all their orders.
questions.business_problem: The account management team wants to identify the company's most valuable customers by revenue, in order to prioritize relationship management and retention efforts on the accounts that matter most.
requirements: Identify the 10 customers who have generated the highest total discounted revenue across all their orders.
questions.reference_query:
SELECT
    cu.customer_id,
    cu.company_name,
    ROUND(SUM(od.unit_price * od.quantity * (1 - od.discount))::numeric, 2) AS total_revenue
FROM customers cu
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = cu.customer_id
JOIN order_details od ON od.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY cu.customer_id, cu.company_name
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC
LIMIT 10;

questions.title: Top 5 Employees by Revenue
questions.description: Identify the 5 employees who generated the highest total discounted revenue across all orders they processed.
questions.business_problem: Sales leadership wants to recognize and analyze the top-performing sales employees based on the total revenue they have personally closed, to inform performance reviews and incentive planning.
requirements: Identify the 5 employees who generated the highest total discounted revenue across all orders they processed.
questions.reference_query:
SELECT
    e.employee_id,
    e.first_name,
    e.last_name,
    ROUND(SUM(od.unit_price * od.quantity * (1 - od.discount))::numeric, 2) AS total_revenue
FROM employees e
JOIN orders o ON o.employee_id = e.employee_id
JOIN order_details od ON od.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY e.employee_id, e.first_name, e.last_name
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC
LIMIT 5;

questions.title: Top 5 Customers by Number of Orders
questions.description: Identify the 5 customers who placed the highest number of distinct orders.
questions.business_problem: Operations wants to understand which customers order most *frequently* — a different signal than total revenue, useful for identifying high-frequency, potentially lower-basket-size accounts versus high-value/low-frequency ones.
requirements: Identify the 5 customers who placed the highest number of distinct orders.
questions.reference_query:
SELECT
    cu.customer_id,
    cu.company_name,
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS order_count
FROM customers cu
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = cu.customer_id
GROUP BY cu.customer_id, cu.company_name
ORDER BY order_count DESC
LIMIT 5;

questions.title: Customers Above Average Revenue
questions.description: Return all customers whose total revenue is strictly greater than the average total revenue computed across all customers.
questions.business_problem: Finance wants to flag customers whose lifetime revenue exceeds the average revenue across all customers, to separate above-average accounts from the long tail for targeted upsell campaigns.
requirements: Return all customers whose total revenue is strictly greater than the average total revenue computed across all customers.
questions.reference_query:
WITH customer_revenue AS (
    SELECT
        cu.customer_id,
        cu.company_name,
        SUM(od.unit_price * od.quantity * (1 - od.discount)) AS total_revenue
    FROM customers cu
    JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = cu.customer_id
    JOIN order_details od ON od.order_id = o.order_id
    GROUP BY cu.customer_id, cu.company_name
)
SELECT *
FROM customer_revenue
WHERE total_revenue > (SELECT AVG(total_revenue) FROM customer_revenue)
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;

questions.title: Employees Above Average Revenue
questions.description: Return all employees whose total revenue exceeds the average total revenue computed across all employees.
questions.business_problem: Sales management wants to identify which employees are performing above the team's average revenue contribution, to recognize strong performers.
requirements: Return all employees whose total revenue exceeds the average total revenue computed across all employees.
questions.reference_query:
WITH employee_revenue AS (
    SELECT
        e.employee_id,
        e.first_name,
        e.last_name,
        SUM(od.unit_price * od.quantity * (1 - od.discount)) AS total_revenue
    FROM employees e
    JOIN orders o ON o.employee_id = e.employee_id
    JOIN order_details od ON od.order_id = o.order_id
    GROUP BY e.employee_id, e.first_name, e.last_name
)
SELECT *
FROM employee_revenue
WHERE total_revenue > (SELECT AVG(total_revenue) FROM employee_revenue)
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;

questions.title: Customers Above Average Order Count
questions.description: Return all customers whose order count exceeds the average order count computed across all customers.
questions.business_problem: Operations wants to identify customers who order more frequently than the typical customer, to understand engagement patterns separate from revenue value.
requirements: Return all customers whose order count exceeds the average order count computed across all customers.
questions.reference_query:
WITH customer_orders AS (
    SELECT
        cu.customer_id,
        cu.company_name,
        COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count
    FROM customers cu
    JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = cu.customer_id
    GROUP BY cu.customer_id, cu.company_name
)
SELECT *
FROM customer_orders
WHERE order_count > (SELECT AVG(order_count) FROM customer_orders)
ORDER BY order_count DESC;

questions.title: Top Categories by Number of Orders
questions.description: Identify the 5 categories that appear in the highest number of distinct orders.
questions.business_problem: Merchandising wants to know which product categories appear in the most customer orders, as a measure of category reach/popularity distinct from raw revenue.
requirements: Identify the 5 categories that appear in the highest number of distinct orders.
questions.reference_query:
SELECT
    c.category_id,
    c.category_name,
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS order_count
FROM categories c
JOIN products p ON p.category_id = c.category_id
JOIN order_details od ON od.product_id = p.product_id
JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = od.order_id
GROUP BY c.category_id, c.category_name
ORDER BY order_count DESC
LIMIT 5;

questions.title: Customers Purchasing from Most Categories
questions.description: Identify the 10 customers who have purchased from the highest number of distinct product categories.
questions.business_problem: The merchandising team wants to identify customers with the broadest purchasing range across product categories — a useful signal for cross-sell health versus customers concentrated in a single category.
requirements: Identify the 10 customers who have purchased from the highest number of distinct product categories.
questions.reference_query:
SELECT
    cu.customer_id,
    cu.company_name,
    COUNT(DISTINCT p.category_id) AS category_count
FROM customers cu
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = cu.customer_id
JOIN order_details od ON od.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN products p ON p.product_id = od.product_id
GROUP BY cu.customer_id, cu.company_name
ORDER BY category_count DESC
LIMIT 10;

questions.title: Revenue by Shipper
questions.description: Calculate the total discounted revenue of orders handled by each shipping company.
questions.business_problem: Logistics and procurement want to understand how much order revenue flows through each shipping partner, to support shipper contract negotiations and performance comparisons.
requirements: Calculate the total discounted revenue of orders handled by each shipping company.
questions.reference_query:
SELECT
    s.shipper_id,
    s.company_name,
    ROUND(SUM(od.unit_price * od.quantity * (1 - od.discount))::numeric, 2) AS total_revenue
FROM shippers s
JOIN orders o ON o.ship_via = s.shipper_id
JOIN order_details od ON od.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY s.shipper_id, s.company_name
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;

questions.title: Employees by Unique Customers Served
questions.description: Identify how many unique customers each employee has handled orders for, ranked from highest to lowest.
questions.business_problem: HR and sales leadership want to evaluate employee reach by counting how many distinct customers each employee has served, as a measure of relationship breadth separate from revenue volume.
requirements: Identify how many unique customers each employee has handled orders for, ranked from highest to lowest.
questions.reference_query:
SELECT
    e.employee_id,
    e.first_name,
    e.last_name,
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.customer_id) AS unique_customers
FROM employees e
JOIN orders o ON o.employee_id = e.employee_id
GROUP BY e.employee_id, e.first_name, e.last_name
ORDER BY unique_customers DESC;

questions.title: Products Sold Above Category Average Quantity
questions.description: Find products whose total quantity sold exceeds the average quantity sold by products *within the same category* (not the company-wide average).
questions.business_problem: Inventory planning wants to identify which products are outperforming their own category's typical sales volume, to inform restocking priorities within each category rather than comparing unrelated categories directly.
requirements: Find products whose total quantity sold exceeds the average quantity sold by products *within the same category* (not the company-wide average).
questions.reference_query:
WITH product_qty AS (
    SELECT
        p.product_id,
        p.product_name,
        p.category_id,
        SUM(od.quantity) AS total_qty
    FROM products p
    JOIN order_details od ON od.product_id = p.product_id
    GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name, p.category_id
),
category_avg AS (
    SELECT
        category_id,
        AVG(total_qty) AS avg_qty_in_category
    FROM product_qty
    GROUP BY category_id
)
SELECT
    pq.product_id,
    pq.product_name,
    pq.category_id,
    pq.total_qty,
    ca.avg_qty_in_category
FROM product_qty pq
JOIN category_avg ca ON ca.category_id = pq.category_id
WHERE pq.total_qty > ca.avg_qty_in_category
ORDER BY pq.category_id, pq.total_qty DESC;

questions.title: Highest Revenue Product per Category
questions.description: For every category, return the product(s) generating the highest revenue within that category, including all products tied for first place.
questions.business_problem: Category managers want to know the single best-selling product (by revenue) within each category, to understand category 'anchor' products and feature them in marketing. Ties must be handled gracefully rather than arbitrarily picking one winner.
requirements: For every category, return the product(s) generating the highest revenue within that category, including all products tied for first place.
questions.reference_query:
WITH product_revenue AS (
    SELECT
        p.product_id,
        p.product_name,
        p.category_id,
        SUM(od.unit_price * od.quantity * (1 - od.discount)) AS total_revenue
    FROM products p
    JOIN order_details od ON od.product_id = p.product_id
    GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name, p.category_id
),
ranked AS (
    SELECT
        pr.*,
        RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category_id ORDER BY total_revenue DESC) AS rnk
    FROM product_revenue pr
)
SELECT
    category_id,
    product_id,
    product_name,
    ROUND(total_revenue::numeric, 2) AS total_revenue
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk = 1
ORDER BY category_id;

questions.title: Customers Above Average Orders (Correlated Subquery)
questions.description: Return customers whose order count exceeds the average order count across all customers, computed via a subquery referenced directly inside `HAVING`.
questions.business_problem: Same business need as Q8 — identify customers ordering more frequently than average — but solved using `HAVING` with a non-correlated scalar subquery, to compare against the CTE-based approach.
requirements: Return customers whose order count exceeds the average order count across all customers, computed via a subquery referenced directly inside `HAVING`.
questions.reference_query:
SELECT
    cu.customer_id,
    cu.company_name,
    COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count
FROM customers cu
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = cu.customer_id
GROUP BY cu.customer_id, cu.company_name
HAVING COUNT(o.order_id) > (
    SELECT AVG(order_count)
    FROM (
        SELECT COUNT(order_id) AS order_count
        FROM orders
        GROUP BY customer_id
    ) sub
)
ORDER BY order_count DESC;

questions.title: Customers Above Average Revenue (Correlated Subquery)
questions.description: Return customers whose total revenue exceeds the average revenue across all customers, using a `HAVING` clause referencing a subquery.
questions.business_problem: Same business need as Q6 — flag above-average-revenue customers — solved via `HAVING` and a nested subquery rather than a CTE, for comparison.
requirements: Return customers whose total revenue exceeds the average revenue across all customers, using a `HAVING` clause referencing a subquery.
questions.reference_query:
SELECT
    cu.customer_id,
    cu.company_name,
    SUM(od.unit_price * od.quantity * (1 - od.discount)) AS total_revenue
FROM customers cu
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = cu.customer_id
JOIN order_details od ON od.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY cu.customer_id, cu.company_name
HAVING SUM(od.unit_price * od.quantity * (1 - od.discount)) > (
    SELECT AVG(rev)
    FROM (
        SELECT SUM(od2.unit_price * od2.quantity * (1 - od2.discount)) AS rev
        FROM orders o2
        JOIN order_details od2 ON od2.order_id = o2.order_id
        GROUP BY o2.customer_id
    ) sub
)
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;

questions.title: Employees Above Average Revenue (Correlated Subquery)
questions.description: Return employees whose total revenue exceeds the average revenue across all employees, using a `HAVING` clause referencing a subquery.
questions.business_problem: Same business need as Q7 — flag above-average-revenue employees — solved via `HAVING` and a nested subquery rather than a CTE.
requirements: Return employees whose total revenue exceeds the average revenue across all employees, using a `HAVING` clause referencing a subquery.
questions.reference_query:
SELECT
    e.employee_id,
    e.first_name,
    e.last_name,
    SUM(od.unit_price * od.quantity * (1 - od.discount)) AS total_revenue
FROM employees e
JOIN orders o ON o.employee_id = e.employee_id
JOIN order_details od ON od.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY e.employee_id, e.first_name, e.last_name
HAVING SUM(od.unit_price * od.quantity * (1 - od.discount)) > (
    SELECT AVG(rev)
    FROM (
        SELECT SUM(od2.unit_price * od2.quantity * (1 - od2.discount)) AS rev
        FROM orders o2
        JOIN order_details od2 ON od2.order_id = o2.order_id
        GROUP BY o2.employee_id
    ) sub
)
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;

questions.title: Customer Revenue Above Employee Average
questions.description: For each employee, return the customers whose revenue (from orders handled by that employee) exceeds the average revenue of all customers handled by that same employee.
questions.business_problem: Sales management wants, for every employee, to identify which of *their* customers generate above-average revenue *relative to that employee's own customer base* — not relative to the company as a whole. This supports per-employee account prioritization.
requirements: For each employee, return the customers whose revenue (from orders handled by that employee) exceeds the average revenue of all customers handled by that same employee.
questions.reference_query:
WITH employee_customer_revenue AS (
    SELECT
        o.employee_id,
        o.customer_id,
        SUM(od.unit_price * od.quantity * (1 - od.discount)) AS revenue
    FROM orders o
    JOIN order_details od ON od.order_id = o.order_id
    GROUP BY o.employee_id, o.customer_id
)
SELECT
    ecr.employee_id,
    ecr.customer_id,
    ROUND(ecr.revenue::numeric, 2) AS revenue
FROM employee_customer_revenue ecr
WHERE ecr.revenue > (
    SELECT AVG(ecr2.revenue)
    FROM employee_customer_revenue ecr2
    WHERE ecr2.employee_id = ecr.employee_id   -- correlation
)
ORDER BY ecr.employee_id, ecr.revenue DESC;

questions.title: Customers Above Average Revenue Using CTE
questions.description: Use a CTE to calculate per-customer revenue, and a second CTE to calculate the overall average, then return customers exceeding that average.
questions.business_problem: Restating Q6's business need with an explicit two-CTE structure — one CTE for customer revenue, a second CTE purely for the overall average — to demonstrate clean CTE composition as a readability pattern.
requirements: Use a CTE to calculate per-customer revenue, and a second CTE to calculate the overall average, then return customers exceeding that average.
questions.reference_query:
WITH customer_revenue AS (
    SELECT
        cu.customer_id,
        cu.company_name,
        SUM(od.unit_price * od.quantity * (1 - od.discount)) AS total_revenue
    FROM customers cu
    JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = cu.customer_id
    JOIN order_details od ON od.order_id = o.order_id
    GROUP BY cu.customer_id, cu.company_name
),
overall_avg AS (
    SELECT AVG(total_revenue) AS avg_revenue
    FROM customer_revenue
)
SELECT cr.*
FROM customer_revenue cr, overall_avg oa
WHERE cr.total_revenue > oa.avg_revenue
ORDER BY cr.total_revenue DESC;

questions.title: Top 5 Customers by Revenue Using CTE
questions.description: Use a CTE to calculate per-customer revenue, then return the top 5 customers by revenue from that CTE.
questions.business_problem: Restating Q3's business need using an explicit CTE rather than a direct aggregation query, to demonstrate the CTE pattern for simple top-N reporting.
requirements: Use a CTE to calculate per-customer revenue, then return the top 5 customers by revenue from that CTE.
questions.reference_query:
WITH customer_revenue AS (
    SELECT
        cu.customer_id,
        cu.company_name,
        SUM(od.unit_price * od.quantity * (1 - od.discount)) AS total_revenue
    FROM customers cu
    JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = cu.customer_id
    JOIN order_details od ON od.order_id = o.order_id
    GROUP BY cu.customer_id, cu.company_name
)
SELECT *
FROM customer_revenue
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC
LIMIT 5;

questions.title: Employees Above Average Revenue Using Multiple CTEs
questions.description: Calculate employee revenue in one CTE, average revenue in a second CTE, and join them using the comparison itself as the join condition.
questions.business_problem: Restating Q7's business need using a two-CTE structure (employee revenue, then average revenue), joined together with an explicit `JOIN ... ON` condition that doubles as the filter.
requirements: Calculate employee revenue in one CTE, average revenue in a second CTE, and join them using the comparison itself as the join condition.
questions.reference_query:
WITH employee_revenue AS (
    SELECT
        e.employee_id,
        e.first_name,
        e.last_name,
        SUM(od.unit_price * od.quantity * (1 - od.discount)) AS total_revenue
    FROM employees e
    JOIN orders o ON o.employee_id = e.employee_id
    JOIN order_details od ON od.order_id = o.order_id
    GROUP BY e.employee_id, e.first_name, e.last_name
),
avg_revenue AS (
    SELECT AVG(total_revenue) AS avg_rev
    FROM employee_revenue
)
SELECT er.*
FROM employee_revenue er
JOIN avg_revenue ar ON er.total_revenue > ar.avg_rev
ORDER BY er.total_revenue DESC;

questions.title: Top Employee by Revenue Using 3 CTEs
questions.description: Find the employee(s) with the single highest total revenue, using a layered three-CTE structure: aggregate, find the maximum, then filter to matches.
questions.business_problem: Leadership wants to identify the single highest-revenue employee company-wide, with the requirement that ties be handled correctly — if two employees are exactly tied for first, both should be returned, not an arbitrary one.
requirements: Find the employee(s) with the single highest total revenue, using a layered three-CTE structure: aggregate, find the maximum, then filter to matches.
questions.reference_query:
WITH employee_revenue AS (
    SELECT
        e.employee_id,
        e.first_name,
        e.last_name,
        SUM(od.unit_price * od.quantity * (1 - od.discount)) AS total_revenue
    FROM employees e
    JOIN orders o ON o.employee_id = e.employee_id
    JOIN order_details od ON od.order_id = o.order_id
    GROUP BY e.employee_id, e.first_name, e.last_name
),
max_revenue AS (
    SELECT MAX(total_revenue) AS max_rev
    FROM employee_revenue
),
ranked_employees AS (
    SELECT er.*
    FROM employee_revenue er
    JOIN max_revenue mr ON er.total_revenue = mr.max_rev
)
SELECT
    employee_id,
    first_name,
    last_name,
    ROUND(total_revenue::numeric, 2) AS total_revenue
FROM ranked_employees;

questions.title: Best Customer per Employee
questions.description: For every employee, return the customer (or customers, if tied) generating the highest revenue from orders that employee handled.
questions.business_problem: For every employee, sales management wants to know which customer they have generated the most revenue from — their single 'best account' — with ties handled so that no genuinely tied customer is dropped from the result.
requirements: For every employee, return the customer (or customers, if tied) generating the highest revenue from orders that employee handled.
questions.reference_query:
WITH employee_customer_revenue AS (
    SELECT
        o.employee_id,
        o.customer_id,
        SUM(od.unit_price * od.quantity * (1 - od.discount)) AS total_revenue
    FROM orders o
    JOIN order_details od ON od.order_id = o.order_id
    GROUP BY o.employee_id, o.customer_id
),
ranked AS (
    SELECT
        ecr.*,
        RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY employee_id ORDER BY total_revenue DESC) AS rnk
    FROM employee_customer_revenue ecr
)
SELECT
    e.employee_id,
    e.first_name,
    e.last_name,
    r.customer_id,
    cu.company_name,
    ROUND(r.total_revenue::numeric, 2) AS total_revenue
FROM ranked r
JOIN employees e ON e.employee_id = r.employee_id
JOIN customers cu ON cu.customer_id = r.customer_id
WHERE r.rnk = 1
ORDER BY e.employee_id;

questions.title: Highest Revenue Product per Category (CTE + Window Function)
questions.description: For every category, return the product(s) generating the highest revenue within that category, including all ties.
questions.business_problem: Identical business requirement to Q14 — for every category, find the top-revenue product(s), correctly handling ties — placed here in the CTE section to highlight the same pattern as a CTE/window-function technique in its own right.
requirements: For every category, return the product(s) generating the highest revenue within that category, including all ties.
questions.reference_query:
WITH product_revenue AS (
    SELECT
        p.product_id,
        p.product_name,
        p.category_id,
        SUM(od.unit_price * od.quantity * (1 - od.discount)) AS total_revenue
    FROM products p
    JOIN order_details od ON od.product_id = p.product_id
    GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name, p.category_id
),
ranked AS (
    SELECT
        pr.*,
        RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category_id ORDER BY total_revenue DESC) AS rnk
    FROM product_revenue pr
)
SELECT
    c.category_id,
    c.category_name,
    r.product_id,
    r.product_name,
    ROUND(r.total_revenue::numeric, 2) AS total_revenue
FROM ranked r
JOIN categories c ON c.category_id = r.category_id
WHERE r.rnk = 1
ORDER BY c.category_id;

questions.title: Customers and Order Count
questions.description: Return every customer and their total order count, ensuring customers with zero orders still appear in the result with a count of 0, rather than being excluded.
questions.business_problem: The customer success team needs a complete roster of every customer along with their order count — including customers who have never placed a single order, since those are exactly the accounts most in need of outreach.
requirements: Return every customer and their total order count, ensuring customers with zero orders still appear in the result with a count of 0, rather than being excluded.
questions.reference_query:
SELECT
    cu.customer_id,
    cu.company_name,
    COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count
FROM customers cu
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = cu.customer_id
GROUP BY cu.customer_id, cu.company_name
ORDER BY order_count DESC;

questions.title: Customers and Latest Order Date
questions.description: Return every customer along with the date of their most recent order, showing `NULL` for customers who have never placed an order.
questions.business_problem: Customer success wants to track recency of engagement — when each customer last placed an order — while still surfacing customers who have never ordered at all, so they aren't invisible in the report.
requirements: Return every customer along with the date of their most recent order, showing `NULL` for customers who have never placed an order.
questions.reference_query:
SELECT
    cu.customer_id,
    cu.company_name,
    MAX(o.order_date) AS latest_order_date
FROM customers cu
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = cu.customer_id
GROUP BY cu.customer_id, cu.company_name
ORDER BY latest_order_date DESC NULLS LAST;

questions.title: Products and Total Quantity Sold
questions.description: Return every product and the total quantity sold across all orders, displaying 0 for products that have never appeared in any order.
questions.business_problem: Inventory management wants a full product catalog report showing total units sold per product, explicitly showing 0 — not a blank — for products that have never been ordered, so slow-moving inventory is clearly visible.
requirements: Return every product and the total quantity sold across all orders, displaying 0 for products that have never appeared in any order.
questions.reference_query:
SELECT
    p.product_id,
    p.product_name,
    COALESCE(SUM(od.quantity), 0) AS total_quantity_sold
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_details od ON od.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name
ORDER BY total_quantity_sold DESC;

questions.title: Customers with No Orders
questions.description: Return only the customers who have zero orders on record — no aggregation or counts needed, just the filtered list itself.
questions.business_problem: Marketing wants a clean, targeted list of customers who have never placed a single order, to drive a dedicated re-engagement or first-purchase incentive campaign.
requirements: Return only the customers who have zero orders on record — no aggregation or counts needed, just the filtered list itself.
questions.reference_query:
SELECT
    cu.customer_id,
    cu.company_name
FROM customers cu
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = cu.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;

questions.title: Products Never Ordered

questions.title: Employees and Total Revenue
questions.description: Return the employee name and the total revenue attributed to that employee, including employees with zero revenue and a catch-all row for unassigned orders.
questions.business_problem: Generate a report showing all employees and the total revenue generated from the orders they handled. The report must include employees who handled orders, employees who never handled an order, and orders that are not assigned to any employee, so that management gets a complete, unbiased picture of revenue attribution across the sales team.
requirements: Return the employee name and the total revenue attributed to that employee, including employees with zero revenue and a catch-all row for unassigned orders.
questions.reference_query:
SELECT
    e.first_name || ' ' || e.last_name AS employee_name,
    COALESCE(
        ROUND(
            SUM((od.unit_price * od.quantity * (1 - od.discount))::numeric),
            2
        ),
        0
    ) AS total_revenue
FROM employees e
FULL OUTER JOIN orders o
    ON e.employee_id = o.employee_id
FULL OUTER JOIN order_details od
    ON od.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY
    e.first_name,
    e.last_name,
    e.employee_id;

/*
Note — CONCAT vs || NULL behaviour:
CONCAT('a', NULL, 'b')  -> 'ab'   (NULL treated as empty string)
'a' || NULL || 'b'      -> NULL   (NULL propagates through the whole expression)
Use || whenever a NULL component should make the entire result NULL (e.g. to
correctly represent "no employee" rather than a blank/space placeholder).

Note — join chain integrity:
Both joins above must remain FULL OUTER JOIN. Downgrading the second join
(orders -> order_details) to INNER or LEFT JOIN would silently drop any
employee/order row that has no matching order_details row, even though the
first FULL OUTER JOIN preserved it.

Note — ::numeric cast:
ROUND(value, 2) requires `value` to be of type numeric in PostgreSQL. The raw
arithmetic (unit_price * quantity * (1 - discount)) may resolve to double
precision, so the explicit ::numeric cast avoids a "function round(double
precision, integer) does not exist" error.

Expected Output:
| employee_name    | total_revenue |
|-------------------|---------------|
| Nancy Davolio     | 125420.35     |
| Andrew Fuller     | 98452.70      |
| Steven Buchanan   | 0.00          |
| NULL              | 520.00        |

Concepts Used:
- FULL OUTER JOIN (chained)
- COALESCE for zero-default aggregation
- CONCAT vs || NULL-propagation behaviour
- ::numeric cast before ROUND()
- GROUP BY with FULL OUTER JOIN

Complexity:
Medium
*/;

questions.title: Customer Revenue Comparison (Advanced)
questions.description: Return the customer's contact name and their total revenue, restricted to whichever customer(s) generated the single highest revenue amount. If multiple customers are tied for the highest revenue, all tied customers must appear — not just one.
questions.business_problem: The finance team wants a reconciliation report showing all customers and their revenue, followed by an analysis of which customer(s) generated the single highest amount of revenue. The report must first reconcile all three data scenarios — customers who generated revenue, customers with no orders, and orders that exist without a valid customer — before identifying the top performer(s).
requirements: Return the customer's contact name and their total revenue, restricted to whichever customer(s) generated the single highest revenue amount. If multiple customers are tied for the highest revenue, all tied customers must appear — not just one.
questions.subtopic: FULL OUTER JOIN / CTE / Tie-Safe Top-N
questions.reference_query:
with rev as (
    select
        c.contact_name,
        coalesce(
            round(
                sum((od.unit_price * od.quantity * (1 - od.discount))::numeric),
                2
            ),
            0
        ) as total_revenue
    from customers c
    full outer join orders o
        on o.customer_id = c.customer_id
    full outer join order_details od
        on od.order_id = o.order_id
    group by c.contact_name, c.customer_id
)
select
    contact_name,
    total_revenue
from rev
where total_revenue >= (select max(total_revenue) from rev);

/*
Note -- tie-safe pattern generalization:
To extend this to "top N with ties" (e.g. top 3 customers by revenue), replace
the MAX(...) filter with DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total_revenue DESC) inside
the CTE and filter the outer query on rank <= N. DENSE_RANK() is required over
RANK() or ROW_NUMBER() to avoid rank gaps after ties or arbitrary tie-breaking.

Note -- why COALESCE is non-negotiable here specifically:
Unlike previous questions where COALESCE was mostly a display/formatting
concern, here it is a correctness requirement: NULL >= anything evaluates to
UNKNOWN in SQL, so any customer left with a NULL total_revenue would be
silently excluded from the tie-safe comparison, even if they were the true
maximum.
*/;

questions.reference_query:
WITH cte_1 AS
(
    SELECT 'Employee' AS Entity_Type
    FROM employees
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'Supplier' AS Entity_Type

questions.title: Country Entity Counts (UNION ALL)
questions.description: Count customers, suppliers, and employees per country in one result set.
questions.business_problem: Leadership wants a single report of how many customers, suppliers, and employees exist in each country.
requirements: Return country, entity_type, and total_records
Include Customer, Supplier, and Employee entity types
Use UNION ALL to combine sources before aggregating
Sort by country, then entity_type
questions.reference_query:
WITH entities AS (
  SELECT country, 'Customer' AS entity_type FROM customers
  UNION ALL
  SELECT country, 'Supplier' FROM suppliers
  UNION ALL
  SELECT country, 'Employee' FROM employees
)
SELECT country, entity_type, COUNT(*) AS total_records
FROM entities
WHERE country IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY country, entity_type
ORDER BY country, entity_type;

questions.title: Country Totals with Entity Type Pivot
questions.description: Show per-country counts of customers, suppliers, and employees as separate columns.
questions.business_problem: The analytics team wants one row per country with customer_count, supplier_count, and employee_count.
requirements: One row per country
Columns: country, customer_count, supplier_count, employee_count
Countries with any entity should appear
Sort by customer_count descending
questions.reference_query:
WITH entities AS (
  SELECT country, 'Customer' AS entity_type FROM customers
  UNION ALL
  SELECT country, 'Supplier' FROM suppliers
  UNION ALL
  SELECT country, 'Employee' FROM employees
)
SELECT
  country,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE entity_type = 'Customer') AS customer_count,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE entity_type = 'Supplier') AS supplier_count,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE entity_type = 'Employee') AS employee_count
FROM entities
WHERE country IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY country
ORDER BY customer_count DESC;

questions.title: Countries with Both Customers and Suppliers
questions.description: Find countries that have at least one customer and at least one supplier.
questions.business_problem: The Sales Director wants to know which countries have both customers and suppliers.
requirements: At least one customer
At least one supplier
Do not include employees
Return country, customer_count, supplier_count
Sort by customer_count descending
questions.reference_query:
WITH entities AS (
  SELECT country, 'Customer' AS entity_type FROM customers
  UNION ALL
  SELECT country, 'Supplier' FROM suppliers
)
SELECT
  country,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE entity_type = 'Customer') AS customer_count,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE entity_type = 'Supplier') AS supplier_count
FROM entities
WHERE country IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY country
HAVING COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE entity_type = 'Customer') >= 1
   AND COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE entity_type = 'Supplier') >= 1
ORDER BY customer_count DESC;

questions.title: Countries with All Three Entity Types
questions.description: Identify countries that have customers, suppliers, AND employees.
questions.business_problem: Ops wants markets where the company has customers, suppliers, and employees present.
requirements: At least one customer, supplier, and employee per country
Return country and the three counts
Sort by total entities descending
questions.reference_query:
WITH entities AS (
  SELECT country, 'Customer' AS entity_type FROM customers
  UNION ALL
  SELECT country, 'Supplier' FROM suppliers
  UNION ALL
  SELECT country, 'Employee' FROM employees
)
SELECT
  country,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE entity_type = 'Customer') AS customer_count,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE entity_type = 'Supplier') AS supplier_count,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE entity_type = 'Employee') AS employee_count,
  COUNT(*) AS total_entities
FROM entities
WHERE country IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY country
HAVING COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE entity_type = 'Customer') >= 1
   AND COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE entity_type = 'Supplier') >= 1
   AND COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE entity_type = 'Employee') >= 1
ORDER BY total_entities DESC;

questions.title: Customer vs Supplier Presence by Country
questions.description: Classify countries by whether they have customers only, suppliers only, or both.
questions.business_problem: The strategy team wants a presence classification for each country.
requirements: Classify each country as Customers Only, Suppliers Only, or Both
Exclude countries with neither
Return country, customer_count, supplier_count, presence
Sort by presence, then country
questions.reference_query:
WITH entities AS (
  SELECT country, 'Customer' AS entity_type FROM customers
  UNION ALL
  SELECT country, 'Supplier' FROM suppliers
),
agg AS (
  SELECT
    country,
    COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE entity_type = 'Customer') AS customer_count,
    COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE entity_type = 'Supplier') AS supplier_count
  FROM entities
  WHERE country IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY country
)
SELECT
  country,
  customer_count,
  supplier_count,
  CASE
    WHEN customer_count > 0 AND supplier_count > 0 THEN 'Both'
    WHEN customer_count > 0 THEN 'Customers Only'
    ELSE 'Suppliers Only'
  END AS presence
FROM agg
WHERE customer_count > 0 OR supplier_count > 0
ORDER BY presence, country;
